CONCLUSION: Bioabsorbable spacer-assisted high-dose PBT was technically feasible in this selected cohort. However, this small, uncontrolled study cannot establish a low risk of uncommon or late adverse events or support conclusions regarding comparative safety or efficacy.

articles.title: Independent validation of a predictive risk model for contrast-enhancing brain lesions supports enhanced periventricular radiosensitivity and variable proton RBE.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Contrast-enhancing brain lesions (CEBLs) were reported as MR-imaging (MRI) endpoint to assess dose effects in healthy brain tissue following proton radiotherapy (PRT) of low-grade-glioma (LGG) patients. A voxel-level risk model was proposed with absorbed dose (D), dose-averaged linear energy transfer (LETD), and proximity to the ventricular system as risk factors. We validated this model in an independent LGG patient cohort. MATERIAL AND METHODS: LGG patients treated at the same institution but more recently (2015-2019) were considered. For each patient, follow-up MRI data were screened for CEBLs, complication-risk maps were calculated and patient-level NTCPCEBL values were determined according to the original model. Eventually, risk model coefficients were updated by regressing the original logistic model to the validation cohort (validC) data. RESULTS: The validC comprised 112 subjects. Observed CEBL incidence of 21% was the same as in the modelling cohort (modelC); observed number of CEBLs and median lesion volume were considerably smaller in the validC, (NvalidC = 26, NmodelC = 67 and Vmed,validC = 110 mm3, Vmed,modelC = 235 mm3). Good calibration of the original patient-level NTCPCEBL model was obtained in the validC. Update of the model coefficients yielded a more pronounced LETD-effect and a 2.4 times higher odds ratio for the complication risk in the periventricular space (PVS). CONCLUSIONS: The presented validation confirms an enhanced radiosensitivity of the PVS, a variable proton RBE, and supports serial complication characteristics of the brain. This underlines the need for a PRT strategy that actively spares the PVS under consideration of an LETD-dependent proton RBE. CLINICAL TRIAL INFORMATION: The study was approved by the ethics committee of the Heidelberg University Hospital (ethics vote: S-516/2022).

articles.title: Phase I dose-escalation study of stereotactic body radiotherapy with elective nodal irradiation for borderline resectable and unresectable locally advanced pancreatic cancer.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Locoregional recurrence remains a major clinical challenge in borderline resectable (BR) and unresectable locally advanced (UR-LA) pancreatic cancer, even after stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT). This phase I trial evaluated the safety, maximum tolerated dose (MTD), and preliminary efficacy of adding prophylactic elective nodal irradiation (ENI) to 5-fraction SBRT. METHODS: Patients with BR/UR-LAPC were enrolled in a 3 + 3 dose-escalation design. SBRT was delivered in 5 fractions using either adaptive magnetic resonance image-guided radiation therapy or respiratory breath-hold radiotherapy with a fiducial marker. The ENI dose was fixed at 30 Gy in five fractions, while the primary tumor dose increased from Level 1 (35 Gy) to Level 3 (40 Gy). The primary endpoint was acute dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) (any Grade ≥ 3 non-hematological adverse events within 14 days after the completion of SBRT). RESULTS: Twelve patients (BR: 4, LA: 8) were enrolled, 11 of whom had previously received systemic chemotherapy. One patient at Level 1 experienced acute Grade 3 anorexia/nausea requiring hospitalization. No DLTs were observed at Levels 2 and 3, and the MTD was not reached. Three patients with preexisting biliary stents developed subacute Grade 3 cholangitis. No Grade ≥ 3 late adverse events occurred. The median overall survival after SBRT was 17.3 months, and the 1-year locoregional control rate was 75%. CONCLUSION: Five-fraction SBRT with simultaneous 30 Gy ENI was feasible, and the MTD was not reached within the tested dose levels up to 40 Gy. Further prospective studies are needed to evaluate its long-term safety and treatment outcomes.

articles.title: Brenner Tumors of the Ovary: Spectrum of Sonographic Findings: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: The objective of the study is to systematically review the literature on the clinical and sonographic features of ovarian Brenner tumors (BTs) and identify characteristics potentially associated with benign versus borderline or malignant histology. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were systematically searched for studies reporting sonographic findings in histologically confirmed ovarian BTs published between January 2000 and November 2025. Findings were summarized descriptively, and exploratory comparisons were performed between benign Brenner tumors (BBTs) and borderline or malignant BTs. Twenty-six studies (19 case reports and 7 case series) involving 150 tumors in 133 patients were included. Of the tumors, 110 were benign and 40 were borderline (n = 9) or malignant (n = 31). Most tumors contained a solid component (78.0%). Tumor morphology differed between groups (p = .012), and solid components were more frequent in borderline or malignant tumors than in benign tumors (90.0% versus 73.6%; p = .044). Moderate or abundant vascularity was more frequent in borderline or malignant tumors (75.8% versus 28.9%; p < .001), whereas acoustic shadowing was more frequent in benign tumors (75.8% versus 11.4%; p < .001). Calcifications or hyperechoic areas occurred at similar frequencies (58.3% versus 50.0%; p = .434). Ovarian BTs appear to exhibit 2 partially contrasting sonographic phenotypes. Benign tumors are commonly solid, poorly vascularized masses with prominent acoustic shadowing, whereas borderline or malignant tumors tend to show greater morphologic complexity, increased vascularity, and less acoustic shadowing. Vascularity and acoustic shadowing may be useful in preoperative characterization, but prospective studies using standardized ultrasound terminology are needed to validate these observations.

articles.title: Is Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Severity Associated with Subclinical Vascular Changes? An Electrophysiological, Ultrasonographic, and Carotid Intima-Media Thickness-Based Analysis.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare clinical outcomes and median nerve ultrasonographic parameters across electrodiagnostic carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) severity groups and to compare hand strength and carotid intima-media thickness (CIMT) across CTS severity groups and healthy controls. METHODS: In this cross-sectional observational study, 38 female patients with electrodiagnostically confirmed CTS and 14 age-similar healthy controls were included. Patients were classified as having mild (n = 12), moderate (n = 14), or severe (n = 12) CTS according to the severity documented in the original electrodiagnostic reports. Clinical assessment included visual analog scale (VAS), Douleur Neuropathique 4 (DN4), and the Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire. Grip and pinch strengths, median nerve cross-sectional area (CSA) and flattening ratio (FR), and CIMT were assessed. RESULTS: VAS, DN4, Boston SSS/FSS, CSA, and FR differed significantly across CTS severity groups (all p < .001), with generally higher values in more severe CTS. Grip strength differed significantly among groups and was lowest in severe CTS (healthy controls: 25.57 ± 2.19 kg; severe CTS: 11.50 ± 2.58 kg; p < .001). Lateral and tip-pinch strengths were lower in all CTS groups than in healthy controls (p < .001) but did not differ among CTS severity subgroups. Mean CIMT was significantly higher in severe than in mild CTS (0.460 ± 0.038 versus 0.410 ± 0.019 mm; p = .002), while mean CIMT was comparable between the combined CTS group and healthy controls. The severe-mild difference remained significant after adjustment for age (Bonferroni-adjusted p = .008). DISCUSSION: Higher CIMT in severe compared with mild CTS suggests a possible relationship between CIMT and greater electrophysiological severity. Larger studies controlling for cardiovascular risk factors are needed to confirm this association.

Incremental Diagnostic Value of Serum Tumor Markers Beyond Multimodal Ultrasound for BI-RADS Category 4 Breast Lesions: A Retrospective Diagnostic Modeling Study.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To determine the incremental diagnostic value and potential clinical utility of serum tumor markers beyond multimodal ultrasound for differentiating benign from malignant Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System category 4 breast lesions. METHODS: This retrospective diagnostic modeling study included 307 patients with 1 pathologically verified BI-RADS category 4 lesion each. Three nested logistic regression models were evaluated: BI-RADS subcategory alone, multimodal ultrasound comprising clinical and ultrasound variables, and multimodal ultrasound plus normalized serum CA15-3, CEA, CA125, and CYFRA21-1 ratios. Discrimination, calibration, Brier score, integrated discrimination improvement, likelihood-ratio testing, bootstrap internal validation, and decision-curve analysis were assessed. Prespecified analyses evaluated lesions 20 mm or smaller and patients with all 4 markers within reference limits. RESULTS: Of 307 lesions, 184 (59.9%) were malignant. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve increased from 0.875 (95% CI, 0.837-0.913) for BI-RADS alone to 0.920 (95% CI, 0.888-0.952) for multimodal ultrasound and 0.953 (95% CI, 0.931-0.976) after addition of serum markers. Relative to multimodal ultrasound, the combined model improved the AUC by 0.033 (95% CI, 0.013-0.055; p = .002), reduced the Brier score by 0.025 (95% CI, 0.011-0.040; p < .001), and yielded an integrated discrimination improvement of 0.103 (95% CI, 0.069-0.138; p < .001). Bootstrap-corrected AUCs were 0.908 and 0.940, respectively. In lesions 20 mm or smaller, AUC increased from 0.934 to 0.970 (p = .003). In the all-marker-negative subgroup, the corresponding increase from 0.912 to 0.930 was not statistically significant (p = .229), although cohort-derived combined-model tertiles showed malignancy rates of 4.0, 24.5, and 89.8% (p for trend <.001). CONCLUSIONS: Serum tumor markers provided statistically significant incremental information beyond multimodal ultrasound in this BI-RADS category 4 cohort, with a particularly clear improvement among small lesions. The marker-negative risk-stratification findings are exploratory. External validation and prospective assessment of clinical pathways are required before implementation.

articles.title: Virtual non-calcium dual-energy computed tomography for postoperative lumbar spine evaluation following pedicle screw instrumentation.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To compare standard grayscale CT, 140-keV virtual monoenergetic imaging, and virtual non-calcium (VNCa) for detection of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-defined relevant foraminal stenosis, disc protrusion or extrusion, and relevant nerve root compression. METHODS: This retrospective study included patients who underwent dual-energy computed tomography (DECT) on a 128-slice single-tube system and MRI within 1 week between August and December 2025; CT reconstructions were read in consensus. Foraminal stenosis and nerve root compression grades 2-3 were considered imaging-defined relevant findings. Only segments with an MRI confidence score of 5 were included. Diagnostic performance and CT confidence scores were summarized descriptively. RESULTS: Twenty-three patients (mean age, 60 ± 12 years; 15 women) contributed 185 evaluated segments. MRI showed relevant foraminal stenosis in 26 segments and disc protrusion or extrusion and relevant nerve root compression in 18 segments each. Foraminal-stenosis sensitivity was 100.0% (26/26) for VNCa and 92.3% (24/26) for both comparators; specificity was 88.7%, 71.1%, and 72.3% for VNCa, standard CT, and 140-keV CT, respectively. Disc protrusion or extrusion sensitivity was 77.8% (14/18) for VNCa and 11.1% (2/18) for both comparators. Standard CT and VNCa each had 83.3% sensitivity and 97.0% specificity for nerve root compression. CONCLUSION: In this small, selected cohort, VNCa had higher observed specificity for MRI-defined foraminal stenosis and higher observed sensitivity for disc protrusion or extrusion. These exploratory findings require confirmation in larger studies that account for patient-level clustering and include more artifact-limited examinations. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: VNCa reconstruction from an existing DECT examination may complement grayscale CT for evaluating MRI-defined foraminal stenosis and disc protrusion or extrusion following lumbar pedicle screw instrumentation without requiring additional scanning.

articles.title: Association of baseline chest computed tomography (CT) findings with inpatient sputum smear positivity and grade in active pulmonary tuberculosis: a retrospective study.
articles.abstract: AIM: In adults admitted with active pulmonary tuberculosis (TB), smear positivity and grade are practical markers of bacillary burden but may be unavailable during early inpatient assessment. We assessed whether baseline chest computed tomography (CT) findings were associated with smear positivity and higher grade. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We performed a single-centre retrospective study of adults with active pulmonary TB who underwent chest CT within 7 days of admission and sputum smear microscopy within 48 hours. Structured CT variables were extracted, and inter-reader agreement was assessed in a dual-reader subset. Outcomes were smear positivity and ordinal smear grade (Negative, Scanty, 1+, 2+, or 3+). Multivariable logistic and ordered logistic models adjusted for age, body mass index, and diabetes were used. Discrimination of an internally derived routine CT score was evaluated by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). RESULTS: Of 328 patients, 161 (49.1%) were smear positive. Cavity prevalence increased from 29.9% in smear-negative patients to 80.0% in grade 3+ smears, and median CT extent from 19.0% to 34.5%. An extent ≥25% (odds ratio [OR]: 3.05, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.80-5.15), cavity (OR: 2.92, 1.77-4.82), and consolidation (OR: 2.19, 1.32-3.63) were independently associated with smear positivity and higher smear grade (ORs: 3.71, 3.44, and 2.72, respectively). The CT score showed moderate discrimination (AUC: 0.765). Sensitivity analyses were directionally consistent. CONCLUSION: Greater CT extent, cavitation, and consolidation were independently associated with smear positivity and higher grade. These findings support CT features as correlates of smear burden but do not establish a role for CT-directed isolation or microbiologic prioritisation.
